Field Level Media

28 Sep 2026, 10:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Ed Szczepanski)
Rookie Lucas Spence ripped a two-run triple to highlight a four-run third inning, helping the Houston Astros celebrate the American League West title with a 9-0 victory over the Athletics on Sunday in West Sacramento, Calif.
Christian Walker homered to lead off the sixth inning and joined Yainer Diaz, Cam Smith and Jeremy Pena in collecting two hits and an RBI for the Astros (81-81), who won the division for the eighth time in the last 10 seasons.
Third-seeded Houston will host the Chicago White Sox on Tuesday in Game 1 of the best-of-three wild-card series. The Astros went 5-2 against the White Sox this season.
Houston actually captured the AL West title prior to the conclusion of its victory, as the Texas Rangers dropped a 6-4 decision to the Minnesota Twins on Sunday.
Yordan Alvarez went 1-for-4 with an RBI single to boost his batting average to .316, giving him his first batting title.
Lawrence Butler had two of the five hits for the Athletics (64-98), who lost for the ninth time in 12 games.
Phillies 7, Tampa Bay 3
Zack Wheeler pitched six strong innings and Kyle Schwarber drove in two runs as the Phillies clinched their fifth straight postseason berth by beating the Rays.
Bryce Harper and Edmundo Sosa homered for Philadelphia, which had lost its previous four games by the combined score of 23-3. The Phillies finally showed signs of life in Game 162, and now they'll head to Atlanta to face the Braves in the National League wild-card round that begins on Tuesday,
Johnny DeLuca homered twice for Tampa Bay. The Rays earned a bye into the American League Division Series and face the winner of the wild-card series between the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox.
Cubs 6, Red Sox 2
Alex Bregman went 4-for-4 with two home runs and four RBIs against his former team to help Chicago wrap up the regular season by defeating Boston in St. Petersburg, Fla.
The game was scheduled to be played in Boston, but was moved to Tropicana Field because of the nor'easter that hit much of New England throughout the weekend.
Both of Bregman's home runs came against Boston starter Tanner Houck, who made his first appearance on the mound since May 2025. Houck (0-1), who had Tommy John surgery last year, allowed three runs on four hits in three innings. The Red Sox were held to five hits and were 0-for-7 with runners in scoring position.
Twins 6, Rangers 4
Josh Bell hit a two-run home run and drove in three to lead host Minnesota to a season-ending win over Texas.
The loss eliminated the Rangers from the American League West title race and the playoffs. Rangers starter Mackenzie Gore allowed one hit and one run in 2 1/3 innings.
Twins starter Dean Kremer (5-5) gave up three hits and one run in seven innings. Kremer yielded a home run to Danny Jansen, but did not allow another Texas runner past first base.
Dodgers 5, Giants 1 (10 innings)
Andy Pages capped a four-run 10th inning with a three-run home run, and visiting Los Angeles beat San Francisco to earn its 100th win of the season.
The Dodgers took the lead in the 10th when Alex Call's two-out double off the left field fence drove in automatic runner Miguel Rojas. The Giants then elected to walk Max Muncy, before Pages foiled that strategy by driving a pitch by Duncan Davitt (0-1) into the left field bleachers for his 23rd home run of the season.
Alex Vesia (3-1), whose perfect ninth sent the game into the 10th, was credited with the win, which allows the Dodgers to take a three-game winning streak into their National League Division Series opener next Saturday against the winner of the wild-card series between the host Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies.
Marlins 5, Braves 3
Heriberto Hernandez and Griffin Conine slugged solo home runs, giving host Miami a win over Atlanta to end its season on a high note.
Marlins ace Sandy Alcantara tossed a scoreless ninth inning for his third career save. It was a fitting end of the year for Alcantara, who threw both the first and last pitch of the season for Miami. sStarter Janson Junk left with a no-decision. He allowed three hits and one run in 4 2/3 innings. Michael Petersen (4-4) earned the win with 1 1/3 hitless innings of relief.
Braves starter JR Ritchie (1-5) took the loss. He allowed seven hits and four runs in 5 2/3 innings. Mauricio Dubon hit his 12th homer to open the scoring and added an RBI single for Atlanta, which begins its home wild-card series against divisional rival Philadelphia on Tuesday.
Nationals 6, Mets 4
Andres Chaparro had three hits, including two solo home runs, and host Washington beat New York to end its season with a series win.
Will Dion (3-2) pitched two scoreless innings for the victory and Erik Tolman worked the ninth for his fifth save for Washington, which improved by 11 wins over 2025.
Francisco Lindor hit his 300th career homer and Ronny Mauricio smacked his third home run in two games for the Mets, who finished last in the National League East. Carson Benge ended his rookie season with three hits and an RBI.
Blue Jays 5, Reds 1
In potentially his final career start, Max Scherzer struck out seven over seven-plus innings and host Toronto topped Cincinnati.
The 42-year-old Scherzer (4-9) allowed one run and six hits to earn his 225th career win and boost his strikeout total to 3,557. The Blue Jays' 37-year-old designated hitter George Springer, who might have also played his last game, like Scherzer received a standing ovation when he was replaced.
Brandon Valenzuela hit a two-run home run for Toronto and Charles McAdoo added a solo shot in the rubber match of the three-game series. Brandon Williamson (5-5) allowed four runs and four hits in three innings for the Reds.
White Sox 4, Rockies 2
Randal Grichuk and Brenton Doyle smacked two-run home runs and Anthony Kay pitched five strong innings to boost host Chicago past Colorado.
The White Sox are set to visit the American League West champion Houston Astros on Tuesday in the opener of an AL wild-card series. Chicago clinched its first playoff berth on Thursday since 2021 but was eliminated from contention for an AL Central title with Saturday's loss to Colorado and a Cleveland victory at Kansas City.
Cole Carrigg homered for Colorado, which finished with more than 100 losses for the fourth successive season.
Royals 3, Guardians 2
Vinnie Pasquantino's second solo homer of the day broke an eighth-inning tie and sent host Kansas City to a win over Cleveland.
Jac Caglianone and Kyle Isbel each had two hits for the Royals, who ended a disappointing 2026 campaign by avoiding a sweep and winning for just the seventh time in the final 25 games.
Daniel Schneemann and Jo Adell each homered and had two hits apiece for the Guardians, who rested key regulars Steven Kwan, Jose Ramirez and Brayan Rocchio one day after securing their third consecutive American League Central title. Cleveland plays either the Chicago White Sox or Houston Astros in the American League Division Series.
Pirates 4, Tigers 2
Jared Jones pitched four innings of one-hit ball and Konnor Griffin led off the game with a solo home run and drove in two runs to lead Pittsburgh past host Detroit.
Griffin's homer was the sixth of his rookie season and helped the Pirates secure their first winning record since 2018 and only their second since last making the postseason in 2015. Jones was not eligible for the win after exiting the game before the fifth. Jones finished 5-6 with a 3.72 ERA in 21 starts after returning from elbow surgery in late May.
Rookie River Ryan (0-1) made his second start for the Tigers and sixth of his career. The right-hander allowed two runs on three hits over 1 1/3 innings. Detroit finished with a losing record after advancing to the American League Division Series each of the past two seasons.
Padres 9, Diamondbacks 4
Gavin Sheets homered and Freddy Fermin knocked in three runs as host San Diego tuned up for their National League wild-card series by stopping visiting Arizona.
San Diego, which opens its best-of-three series Tuesday night against the visiting Chicago Cubs, snapped a 4-4 tie with three runs in the bottom of the seventh. Fermin capped it with a two-run single.
Michael Soroka pitched 4 2/3 innings for Arizona, which was eliminated from postseason contention when Philadelphia beat Tampa Bay around the same time San Diego's Jake Cronenworth drew a bases-loaded walk to push home the go-ahead run in the seventh.
Brewers 6, Cardinals 4
Jacob Misiorowski strengthened his case for the National League Cy Young Award, allowing just two hits over five-plus scoreless innings, as host Milwaukee beat St. Louis to close with five consecutive wins and its franchise record for victories in a season (103).
Misiorowski (16-5) allowed two singles in 5 1/3 innings and lowered his major league-leading ERA to 1.80. The right-hander struck out five, giving him 252 strikeouts for the year.
Cardinals starter Andre Pallante (12-9) allowed six runs on 10 hits in five innings. He allowed six singles in the first inning for a 3-0 Brewers lead as well as Gary Sanchez's home run in the third.
Mariners 7, Angels 4
Logan Gilbert pitched four-plus hitless innings and struck out eight as host Seattle dealt Los Angeles its 100th loss of the season. It was also the last game for Dan Wilson as the Mariners' manager. The team announced after the game that Wilson will not return in that role in 2027 after a disappointing season and third-place finish in the American League West.
Jose Siri homered for the Angels, losers of 100 games for the first time. They had been the lone active MLB team to never suffer that many defeats.
Gilbert didn't allow a baserunner until walking Moises Ballesteros leading off the fifth. He struck out the side in the first inning to reach 200 strikeouts for the season, becoming the fourth pitcher in franchise history to do so in multiple seasons.

item.content:encoded:
5 men arrested near UK air base used by US in Iran war on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act
LONDON (AP) — U.K. police said that five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran are being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
London’s Metropolitan Police, which takes the lead on potential terrorist activities, said police received a call at 12:45 a.m. related to the three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward RAF Fairford, a U.K.-owned base that is operated by the U.S. under an agreement dating back to the Cold War.
The arrests come at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states to the U.K., with Russia and Iran among those that have used proxies to commit crimes on their behalf on British soil. In March, officials said the number of national security cases involving activity by hostile states including Iran increased 50% in the six months to December 2025.
Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iranian missile sites under an agreement with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who voiced opposition to the war after it was launched by the U.S. and Israel on Feb. 28.
Authorities are investigating a link between the Fairford arrests and Iran as one possibility. Iran has previously indicated that a base used to attack its territory is a legitimate target.
Powerful nor’easter floods Northeast again, causing problems from New Jersey to New England
BOSTON (AP) — Residents of coastal communities in the Northeast slogged through floodwaters for a second day as a powerful nor’easter pummeled the shoreline Sunday, knocking out power to tens of thousands of homes.
Tidal surges swamped low-lying neighborhoods in New Jersey while wind gusts toppled trees on New York's Long Island, damaging homes and bringing down utility poles.
In the New Jersey beach town of Sea Bright, each high tide brought a new round of flooding. “It's not like a one-time occurrence,” said Caroline Virenius, whose garage filled with about a foot of water (30 centimeters). “It's getting wet again and again.”
The slow-moving storm, which killed a New York City Housing Authority worker when a tree fell Saturday, was expected to linger through Sunday with heavy rain, strong winds and dangerous surf all the way to New England.
Extreme amounts of rain — more than 4 inches (10 centimeters) since Friday in some spots in New Jersey — combined with a surging ocean led to flooding amounts not seen for close to a decade in places used to dealing with high water, residents said.
Mexico's Baja California braces for major Hurricane Polo as Hurricane Nolo still threatens Hawaii
HILO, Hawaii (AP) — Hurricane Nolo edged further away from the Hawaiian Islands on Sunday as major Hurricane Polo bore down on Mexico's southern Baja California peninsula with a threat of storm surge, high winds and heavy rains.
Nolo was well southwest of Hawaii and moving away from the Big Island as the weekend drew to a close. A high-wind warning, wind advisory and high surf advisory remained in effect for parts of the island through Sunday evening as Nolo’s maximum sustained winds increased to near 105 mph (165 kph).
Meanwhile, residents of Mexico's Baja California braced for the expected arrival Monday of Category 3 Polo, which had top sustained winds of 125 mph (205 kph) Sunday evening, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said. Heavy rainfall from Polo would begin impacting the peninsula overnight and could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Forecasters said Polo would hit the Mexican mainland after crossing Baja California and could bring heavy rain and flooding to parts of the U.S. Southwest later in the week. Polo was moving to the north at 12 mph (19 kph) about 270 miles (435 kilometers) west of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, the hurricane center said.
Forecasters said Nolo's outer bands could cause life-threatening flooding and mudslides, with parts of the Big Island possibly getting up to 20 inches (50 centimeters) of rain. Heavy rain also was expected on the other islands.
Pope blasts assisted dying as 'false compassion' at French shrine known for miraculous cures
LOURDES, France (AP) — Pope Leo XIV on Sunday condemned the legalization of medically assisted death as immoral “false compassion,” reaffirming Catholic teaching on the sanctity of life during a visit to Lourdes, the French shrine associated with miraculous healings.
On the third day of his visit to France, Leo again waded into the end-of-life debate unfolding in his native U.S. and countries around the world. The issue roiled French politics for years before lawmakers recently approved legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication.
Leo also met on Sunday with seven survivors of clergy sexual abuse, in what has now become a regular appointment for popes on foreign visits. The aim is to atone for the Catholic Church’s failure to protect its youngest and most vulnerable members from predator priests.
“It was extraordinary,” said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos, who joined four others at a press conference afterward to praise Leo for the encounter, saying he listened and was informed of their cases. “I never thought I would have a pope before me.”
Leo’s visit to the once staunchly Catholic and officially secular France has been marked by huge crowds — 800,000 at Leo’s Mass on Paris’ iconic Place de la Concorde — and his messaging against abortion and assisted dying.
Palestinian death toll in Gaza war passes 74,000, and other Mideast news
The Palestinian death toll from the nearly three-year Israel-Hamas war has surpassed 74,000, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
Meanwhile, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Tehran has not been formally notified of U.S. President Donald Trump's rejection of its proposed deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. And the World Health Organization says nearly 700 people have been killed in Yemen since fighting escalated last month.
Here is a look at the latest news from the Middle East on Sunday.
Araghchi said Tehran awaits a U.S. response through mediators after Trump rejected Iran’s proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume negotiations.
Speaking from New York, Araghchi told NBC that Iran is “fully prepared for the war to be resumed."
Anthropic and OpenAI sound the alarm on AI safety — and seek to shape how it's controlled
SAN FRANCISCO (AP) — As tech titans warned an AI-weary world that their own advanced systems could endanger humanity, the question emerged: What do they have to gain?
The answer may lie in the companies’ efforts to score political goals ahead of the U.S. midterm elections and the money top artificial intelligence labs and their investors stand to make in much-anticipated listings on a jittery stock market.
The CEOs of Anthropic and OpenAI recently declared America’s cutting-edge models are so powerful, they’re dangerous, and need to be regulated and independently tested before being released. In a rare instance of unity, they have sketched alarming scenarios in essays, social media posts and speeches to the United Nations.
Along the way, they are shaping the conversation around how their technology should be controlled. With their rhetoric, the companies appear to be seeking public favor and to set the terms for their own safety protocols in the unregulated market, experts, analysts and former government evaluators told The Associated Press.
Those aims may not exactly align with what Anthropic engineer Jacob Coxon sought when he quit via a post on X this month, calling for a pause on tech development to keep “superhuman” systems from eluding their makers' control. But the companies saw his post as an opportunity to highlight their own safety efforts and position themselves as cautious market leaders, just when they need fresh capital before going public on Wall Street.
Supreme Court vote shadows Maine Sen. Susan Collins in her first race after abortion rights decision
GORHAM, Maine (AP) — For years, Planned Parenthood’s endorsement of Susan Collins was enough to persuade Erin Evans to vote for Maine's longtime U.S. senator, believing that the moderate Republican would protect abortion access.
Evans is now “just furious with myself” for those votes. The 56-year-old from Portland described Collins’ critical vote to confirm Brett Kavanaugh to the U.S. Supreme Court, where President Donald Trump's nominee eventually helped overturn the constitutional right to abortion, as a betrayal.
“I was a really uninformed voter,” Evans said. “I thought any woman from Maine was probably in line with me.”
The Nov. 3 election will be the first time Collins is on the ballot since the Supreme Court’s 2022 ruling that overturned Roe v. Wade, resulting in abortion being banned in much of the United States. This time, Evans says she is backing Democrat Troy Jackson, a former state lawmaker and logger trying to deny Collins a sixth term.
Jackson and Democrats are hoping that voters like Evans will help flip a seat in a state the party has made a priority in the quest to retake the Senate.
From collapse to clinch, Phillies survive 'living hell' of last week and win final NL wild card
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Kyle Schwarber belly-flopped more than he actually slid headfirst into second base and popped up with his uniform smudged in dirt. He punched his right fist in the air and shouted something in exhilaration toward a fired-up Phillies dugout.
Schwarber delivered with a clutch two-run double, yes. He also showed the fire, the fight that vanished from the Phillies during a treacherous week that sent them from the brink of a wild-card clinch to the edge — and yes, the bottom was crumbling — of an all-time franchise collapse.
His slide had Phillies fans roaring from their feet — perhaps more than a few who wore brown paper bags over their heads a night earlier — and instantly all felt right on a soggy day inside Citizens Bank Park.
Zack Wheeler pitched a gem against Tampa Bay on Sunday and untangled a few thousand knots inside the stomachs of Phillies fans, and even from those inside a mostly solemn clubhouse. The Phillies survived their perilous five-day scare and are indeed headed to the playoffs for the fifth straight season after beating the Rays 7-3 to clinch the final NL wild-card berth.
“We didn't play the best baseball we could in September,” slugger Bryce Harper said. “Should we have clinched two weeks ago? Probably, right? But we didn't. We clinched today.”
Americans rally in singles to win the Presidents Cup for the 11th straight time
MEDINAH, Ill. (AP) — The deficit was larger than anything the Americans had ever experienced at home in the Presidents Cup. The celebration Sunday afternoon? That was all too familiar, even the part where President Donald Trump stuck around for the trophy presentation.
The U.S. players — from world No. 1 Scottie Scheffler to 21-year-old rookie Jackson Koivun — passed the gold cup down the line, which was only fitting.
Everyone had a hand in the latest comeback at Medinah, where the Americans delivered the most lopsided singles session in Presidents Cup history. They won nine of the 12 matches and halved the other for a 17-13 victory, their 11th in a row against the hard-luck Internationals.
U.S. captain Brandt Snedeker went from blaming himself for the three-point deficit to choking back emotions as his team set the tone early and rode momentum and a raucous Chicago gallery late that left them believing again they can succeed in team golf.
The real proof comes a year from now in Ireland for the Ryder Cup. For now, the Americans redeemed themselves in a competition they have lost only once since these matches began in 1994.
Taylor Swift becomes most-awarded artist in MTV VMAs history, dedicates top prize to Dolly Parton
NEW YORK (AP) — Taylor Swift broke records at the 2026 MTV Video Music Awards, as she is known to do.
The pop powerhouse received the inaugural Artist Director Honors on Sunday night, becoming the most-awarded artist in VMA history.
Previously, she was tied with Beyoncé for the title, with 30 VMAs each. The new award is meant to recognize artists “whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling."
“I got to start making music videos and being a part of music videos 20 years ago,” Swift said in her speech, adding that she's been involved in making roughly 60 music videos, 18 of which she wrote and directed.
“You, the fans, make it so much fun,” she said.

item.description: PHILADELPHIA -- The Phillies celebrated. They popped champagne and beer bottles, smoked cigars and blared music in the home clubhouse on Sunday evening at Citizens Bank Park. It felt cathartic. It represented a fresh start. Last week, the Phillies had a four-game lead over Arizona for the final NL Wild Card spot with five games to play, and no team since postseason play began in 1903 had blown a lead like that. item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA -- The Phillies celebrated.
They popped champagne and beer bottles, smoked cigars and blared music in the home clubhouse on Sunday evening at Citizens Bank Park. It felt cathartic. It represented a fresh start. Last week, the Phillies had a four-game lead over Arizona for the final NL Wild Card spot with five games to play, and no team since postseason play began in 1903 had blown a lead like that.
But the Phillies stumbled. They lost four in a row, while Arizona won four in a row. Suddenly, the Phils needed to beat the Rays on the final day of the 162-game season to punch their ticket to the postseason and avoid being immortalized alongside the 1964 Phillies, who infamously blew a 6 1/2-game lead with 12 to play to lose the NL pennant to St. Louis.
So, they partied. It’s what baseball teams do when they clinch.
“It’s so hard to get here,” Trea Turner said. “We had such an up and down here as a whole team. We were talking about it in the cage earlier today. I think this is the first time I've ever had to play like 162. First time ever, 162 has counted for, you know, a big deal. So I think it's kind of a rare situation, and I'm glad we got the job done.”
It has been a long, trying season in Philadelphia. So regardless of how anybody felt about the past several weeks -- and nobody could argue they played poorly at times -- the Phillies always planned to celebrate this moment.
Gloria Gaynor’s “I Will Survive” was the first song to play in the clubhouse. It was fitting.
“Everything resets,” Bryce Harper said. “You get into October and everything resets obviously.
“We’re the type of team that, you know, we don’t care … like I said, people’s opinions of us or what they think or what anybody thinks about our team. I mean, we're going to go in and do our job and we need to do our job. Obviously, we didn't play the best baseball we could in September. Should we have clinched two weeks ago? Probably. Right? But we didn’t. You know, we clinched today, and that's how the story's written right now.”
The Phillies started the season at 9-19, costing manager Rob Thomson his job on April 28. Don Mattingly took his place.
The Phillies not only rebounded, but they had one of the best records in baseball for months. They looked like a postseason threat, too, because they had Jesús Luzardo, Cristopher Sánchez and Zack Wheeler pitching well atop the rotation and because the offense finally seemed to click following Luis Arraez’s arrival from the Giants on Aug. 3.
But then they stumbled. The offense went from one of the best in baseball in August to one of the worst in September. They scored three runs during the four-game losing streak, which included a 21-inning scoreless streak.
Fans booed.
He allowed one run in six innings as the Phillies took a 7-1 lead.
“We know who we are,” Wheeler said. “We just gotta play like it. At the beginning and at the end, we didn't play like it so much. So we gotta turn it up. We gotta be ready for Atlanta.”
Bryson Stott, starting in the cleanup spot for just the seventh time in his career, hit a two-out double in the first inning to score a run to give the Phillies a 1-0 lead. J.T. Realmuto snapped an 0-for-34 slump with a double to score a run in the second to make it 2-0. Kyle Schwarber’s two-out double scored two runs to make it 4-0.
Harper’s homer in the fifth was the team’s first since Tuesday and Harper’s first since Sept. 12.
Fans cheered.
“Today, that was one of our better crowds, I thought,” Mattingly said. “You don't hear a lot of, ‘Let's go, Phillies!’" at our games. It's just waiting for things. Right? It'd be great if it would be like an uplifting-type scenario. In the Milwaukee series, somebody makes an out in the fourth with a guy on base, and it's like a boo. And I know it's the fans' right to do it, but it's like, you can either lift up or you can hold down, and if you lift the team up, you’ve got a game.”
Alex McFarlane allowed two runs in the seventh, then Luzardo pitched the eighth. He might have been the Phillies’ best pitcher this season, but he hadn’t pitched since Sept. 7 because of inflammation in his left shoulder.
Sunday was the first time he had faced hitters since then.
He retired the side on four pitches. He looked great. He said he’s available to start this week, if asked. If not, he’ll be available in the bullpen. The same is true for Andrew Painter, who is also in play to start this week.
Wheeler? He could pitch in Atlanta, too.
“I feel like I'm prepared to give the team whatever they ask, whatever they need,” Luzardo said.
The Phillies will need to get creative with their pitching to beat Atlanta. They will need their hitters to show up and beat Chris Sale on Tuesday.
It’s not impossible.
“The past is the past,” Luzardo said. “You play 162 games for a reason. I think this team has what it takes, and we obviously showed it throughout a full season. I don't think the last four days are indicative of what we can do. I think today was and I think that we look forward to Tuesday starting with a clean slate.”

The Philadelphia Phillies need a win or an Arizona Diamondbacks loss today to clinch a Wild Card spot in the National League on the regular season's final day. So how did they get here? Well, the Phillies have lost four games in a row and have been outscored 23-3 during this span. They had a 6.5 game lead over the Diamondbacks on Sept. 1, but have gone just 9-14 this month. If the Phillies miss out on the postseason, it will be an epic collapse.
Luckily, Zack Wheeler is taking the mound against the Tampa Bay Rays in a must-win game, so the Phillies have a pretty good shot of clinching a Wild Card berth on Sunday. And if they do so, their superstar player, Bryce Harper, will have a ton of pressure on him this October, according to one rival scout.
Why this postseason means more for Phillies' Bryce Harper
It appears that Harper will be ticketed for the Baseball Hall of Fame when all is said and done and the book is closed on his illustrious career. However, the 33-year-old still has never won a championship in his 15-year MLB tenure.
"Bryce Harper needs a title to complete his resume," one rival NL scout said. "Not sure anyone else has more pressure in regards to their legacy. They have had stacked teams in Philly and the everyday fans know that the Nationals won (a title) after he left."
Harper and the Phillies got close to winning a title in 2022, which saw them lose to the Houston Astros in six games. Harper had his biggest postseason moment with a go-ahead home run against the San Diego Padres in the NLCS, lifting the Phillies to the NL pennant. But the Phillies ultimately came up short in '22 and then again in 2023 when they lost in the NLCS to the Diamondbacks. The Phillies haven't made it past the NLDS since then despite making the playoffs the last two years.
As previously alluded to, the Washington Nationals won the World Series in 2019, which was the same year that Harper left in free agency to sign a 13-year, $330 million deal with the Phillies. As impressive as Harper's career in the majors has been, he still needs to win a title to stamp his legacy as one of the all-time great players.
For that, no one has more pressure on them to perform this postseason. The Phillies need to make it there first, but if they do, Harper must step up and lead his team on a deep run in October.

The Philadelphia Phillies’ lineup has looked completely different since the addition of second baseman Luis Arraez.
While his production hasn’t been as prolific with the Phillies as it was with the San Francisco Giants, having him as protection for Bryce Harper as the cleanup hitter has enabled the Philadelphia star to take his performance to another level.
The contact-first approach that Arraez brings is something the rest of the team bought into. In August, the Phillies had one of the best offenses in the MLB, improving their on-base percentage and coming up with timely hits.
However, Philadelphia looks like it could be without Arraez for the time being after he suffered a lower leg injury in the series finale against the Milwaukee Brewers. With him, the Phillies were placed last among the lineups of playoff contenders by Stephen J. Nesbitt and Chad Jennings of The Athletic (subscription required); without him, they are solidified in that spot.
Where does Phillies lineup rank among playoff contenders?
They placed the team 13th, and it is hard to argue with that placement based on the numbers in 2026. There are a lot of big names in the lineup, but not much production.
Entering the final series of the regular season, there are only two healthy Phillies players who have a wRC+ that is above the league average: Harper, with a team-high 135, and designated hitter Kyle Schwarber, with a 130.
Arraez was third with a 110, and for a lineup that has been so underwhelming for large chunks of the season, losing him creates a major void in the lineup. Right now, the most consistent hitter beyond that duo is probably Alec Bohm, who got off to a historically poor start but has been excellent in the second half.
He has a .312/.379/.445 slash line in 243 plate appearances and is batting over .300 for the second straight month.
Phillies need supporting cast to step up
Will players on the team wake up and turn things around in October? On paper, this is a star-studded group, loaded with All-Stars such as shortstop Trea Turner, catcher J.T. Realmuto and outfielder Brandon Marsh.
Unfortunately, the first two are in the midst of the least productive seasons of their respective careers, and Marsh has been arguably the worst hitter in baseball for nearly three months. Philadelphia desperately needs them, along with Bryson Stott, to catch fire once again as they did in August.
This team has proven capable of getting hot and producing at a high level. But the odds are certainly stacked against them heading into the postseason, especially with Arraez potentially being sidelined.

Luis Arraez suffered an ankle injury on Thursday night against the Milwaukee Brewers and was on the ground in pain afterward.
He exited the game, and it was revealed that his X-rays were negative and that he has an ankle sprain. With the postseason starting on Tuesday and the Phillies fighting for a spot, his status is unclear. While speaking to reporters, interim manager Don Mattingly revealed he is unsure what Arraez's status is moving forward, but he is hopeful he will return.
"I'm hopeful that he's going to play, but we'll see," Mattingly said to reporters after the game, per 97.5 The Fanatic's Colin Newby. "We'll see where it goes."
Arraez was the Phillies' big acquisition at the trade deadline. He is having a career year defensively and has been an elite hitter for his entire career. The Phillies moved Alec Bohm to first base, Bryce Harper to right field and Bryson Stott to third base to accommodate Arraez, but now they are at risk of missing the postseason. The typical recovery time for an ankle sprain would indicate that he will at least miss the Wild Card Series, but the team will further evaluate him on Friday, per Mattingly.
The Phillies still have a two-game lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks for the final Wild Card spot, but without Arraez, things are not looking great. Arraez's batting average has taken a hit since he joined the Phillies, as he is only hitting .278 with a .678 OPS. However, he is still on pace to win his fourth career batting title.
Losing him for the final series could cost the Phillies a postseason spot, and not having him for the Wild Card Series could have an extremely negative impact on their offense. He has 21 RBIs in 46 games with the Phillies and has a .778 OPS this season with runners in scoring position.

The Phillies have turned baseball’s oldest lineup blueprint upside down, and the runs are following, writes Jared Diamond for The Wall Street Journal.
Since reshaping the batting order, Philadelphia has raised its scoring from 4.39 to 4.67 runs per game, jumping from 16th to ninth in MLB.
For generations, the formula barely changed: a high-contact table-setter hit near the top and the biggest power bat hit in the middle.
The Phillies have flipped the script.
Kyle Schwarber, one of baseball’s most feared home-run hitters and also one of its most frequent strikeout victims, now leads off.
Batting cleanup — the spot long reserved for sluggers like Lou Gehrig and Joe DiMaggio — is Luis Arraez, a three-time batting champion with little home-run power who hits behind Bryce Harper.
With the Giants, before Philadelphia acquired him at the trade deadline, Arraez typically batted first or second.
Even manager Don Mattingly acknowledged how strange the alignment would have looked during his playing days in the 1980s and 1990s.
“Things are changing,” Mattingly said.
Phillies president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski said that in an earlier era, a hitter with Arraez’s profile would have been penciled into one of the first two spots almost automatically.
Instead, Philadelphia wants his bat in play with runners aboard, where his .349 career average with runners in scoring position can do the most damage.
The logic is rather than forcing hitters into traditional roles, build the lineup around what each one does best.
As Dombrowski put it, “It does just tell you how the game has changed.”

Brewers record their first 100-win season with victory over Phillies
The Milwaukee Brewers reached 100 wins for the first time, and Jackson Chourio hit his 25th homer to lift them to a 5-1 victory over Philadelphia on Thursday night that slowed the Phillies’ playoff push.
The Phillies needed a win to at least have a shot at clinching their fifth straight trip to the playoffs. They instead can try again to clinch for the third straight game on Friday against Tampa Bay.
Philadelphia played without NL batting leader Luis Arraez after he came off with a sprained left ankle after he tried to avoid a tag at first base.
Milwaukee reached one more milestone to go with its National League Central title and a first-round postseason bye. The Brewers are the first team this year to reach 100 wins and are trying to hold off the defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers for the No. 1 seed in the NL playoffs. Their previous high was 97 wins last year.
Brewers fans crowded the seats behind the dugout and held “100” signs as players left the field.
Bryce Harper tied the game 1-1 with an RBI single in the third.
Jake Bauers hit the tie-breaking single off José Alvarado (5-4) in the eighth inning, and Cooper Pratt and Joey Ortiz added run-scoring singles in the inning for a 4-1 lead. Chourio hit a solo shot in the ninth.
JoJo Romero (3-3) got the win and Antonio Senzatela earned his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter had another terrific outing in a second-half rebound that should see him play a role in the postseason in the rotation or out of the bullpen. He allowed Sam Frelick’s RBI double in the second and finished with eight strikeouts and three walks in six innings.
The rookie right-hander was demoted to the minors in June after a 12-4 loss to Miami left him with eight losses in nine decisions and a 7.06 ERA. Since his July 31 recalled has a 3.65 ERA in 11 starts with 62 strikeouts to 23 walks.
Philadelphia got more good pitching news earlier in the day when All-Star lefty Jesús Luzardo said he has recovered enough from left shoulder inflammation that he should be able to pitch next week in the playoffs.
Up next
Milwaukee tunes up for the playoffs with a three-game homestand against St. Louis.

Brewers take down Phillies for franchise's first 100-win season
(Photo credit: Bill Streicher)
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run Thursday for the Milwaukee Brewers, who reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with their 5-1 win over the hosting Philadelphia Phillies.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5 and added a double, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame. Chourio, who pinch-hit for designated hitter William Contreras, led off the frame with a walk off Jose Alvarado (5-4) and stole second.
Gary Sanchez singled deep to left field to put runners on the corners, and after Alvarado got Luis Lara to line out to shallow center, Cooper Pratt (2-for-3) welcomed Chase Shugart with another hit up the middle to give the Brewers a two-run lead. Joey Ortiz added a two-out hit, a blooper to shallow center that allowed Sanchez to score from second.
Chourio added a solo home run, his 25th blast of the season, in the ninth.
Five Brewers pitchers held the Phillies (87-72) to just four hits. JoJo Romero (3-3) allowed one hit in 1 1/3 innings against St. Louis, who Milwaukee acquired him from last month. Romero picked up his second win with the Brewers since coming off the injured list (appendectomy) earlier this month.
Antonio Senzatela relieved Romero, allowing a walk over the final 1 2/3 innings to earn his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter held the Brewers to just one run over six innings. The rookie allowed five hits and three walks while matching a season-high eight strikeouts. His only blemish came in the second, when Sal Frelick doubled home Sanchez.
Kyle Schwarber (2-for-4) and Bryce Harper (2-for-4) combined to get all four of the Phillies hits. Harper's third-inning single scored Schwarber, who led off the frame with a double off Brewers starter Shane Drohan. Philadelphia managed just one hit, a Schwarber single in the seventh, against the Brewers bullpen.
Besides losing the game, the Phillies may also have lost infielder Luis Arraez, who reportedly sprained an ankle trying to avoid a tag on a groundout in the sixth inning.
With the win, Milwaukee can officially clinch home-field advantage throughout the postseason should the Los Angeles Dodgers lose Thursday night to the visiting San Diego Padres.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two.
--Field Level Media

Bryce Harper
’s road to MLB was different from most teenage prospects. Now an unbelievable amateur talent in Las Vegas, Harper opted to fast-track his education and baseball timeline rather than stay in high school through graduation. The move put him in junior college baseball, and he was younger than most of the players around him.
The decision opened a door few prospects get. Harper earned his GED and enrolled at the College of Southern Nevada, making him eligible for the 2010 MLB Draft at age 17. His performance against older competition quickly made the gamble a defining stage of his development, eventually leading the Washington Nationals to take him with the No. 1 overall pick.
What was Bryce Harper’s bold early move that shaped MLB career?
Harper’s turning point came when he was still in high school in Las Vegas. He didn’t go the traditional high school route, but earned his GED after his sophomore year and enrolled at the College of Southern Nevada. The move was intended to accelerate his eligibility for the MLB Draft.
The decision was important because Harper was getting extraordinary attention even before he entered professional baseball.
He appeared on the cover of Sports Illustrated at age 16, a sign of the expectations that surrounded him. Thus, the early move only served to bring more attention to a teenager who was already being groomed as a potential future MLB star.
The College of Southern Nevada gave Harper something that high school did not: the chance to play against older players and get ready for the 2010 Draft. MLB records show he was just 17 years old during his junior college season, although he was the age of a high school junior.
Still, the move did not guarantee immediate success. Harper stepped into a new world with big expectations and had to adjust to playing against college players. The pressure was pretty high around him for a junior college athlete, with scouts and media watching him like a hawk during his performances.
His reply came by way of production. Harper batted .443 with 31 home runs and 98 RBIs in 66 games for the College of Southern Nevada in 2010. He also had a .526 on-base percentage and .987 slugging percentage for a 1.513 OPS.

Harper’s age and junior college performance made the case that he was ready for professional baseball. When the 2010 MLB Draft arrived, the Washington Nationals picked him first overall.
The Nationals then signed the 17-year-old to a five-year, $9.9 million deal with a $6.25 million signing bonus, according to MLB’s career timeline. The pick achieved the short-term goal of the unconventional educational and baseball choice Harper had made years earlier.
Harper’s progression from junior college to the pros was also rapid. He reached the Majors in 2012 at age 19, was an All-Star and won National League Rookie of the Year. That early acceleration had propelled him from high school prospect to MLB player in a remarkably short period.
Bryce Harper turned teenage pressure into success
The expectations had been building since Harper was a teenager, and the No. 1 overall pick carried them. He was already one of baseball’s most closely tracked prospects thanks to his time in the minors, but joining the Nationals put him in the national spotlight.
When he got to the Majors, Harper quickly answered. He batted .270 with 22 homers and 18 steals in 139 games as a rookie and was the National League Rookie of the Year. He also became the youngest position player drafted to an All-Star Game at the time, aged 19.
The ensuing seasons showed that his success was not confined to his breakout rookie season, along the way, Harper developed as a hitter and learned how to handle MLB pitching, culminating in one of the more celebrated individual seasons of his career in 2015.
Harper’s 2015 campaign was a major milestone. At age 22, he batted .330 with a .460 on-base percentage and .649 slugging percentage, hit 42 home runs and won his first National League MVP Award. MLB says he is the youngest player to ever win the award unanimously.
Bryce Harper built a legacy beyond expectations
After moving to Philadelphia, Harper’s career continued to evolve. In 2021, he posted a 1.044 OPS, 42 doubles and 35 home runs in 141 games, earning his second National League MVP Award.
That second MVP cemented the bridge from his teenage rep to his long-term MLB achievements. Instead of just being a very good No. 1 pick, Harper developed into a guy who piled up major individual awards at different points in his career.
His postseason performances for the Phillies have also become a big part of his career narrative. Harper homered in the game-winning run in Game 5 of the National League Championship Series and was named the NLCS MVP in 2022 before making his World Series debut.
Harper was on the active roster of the Phillies through the 2026 season, adding to his statistical record. MLB’s current player page through the 2026 regular season has 1,949 career hits, 391 home runs, 1,135 RBIs and a .904 career OPS.

So Harper's career began with a decision made long before the MVP awards, the All-Star selections, the postseason moments. Leaving high school early to join the College of Southern Nevada changed the timing of his development, giving him the opportunity to enter the 2010 Draft at 17. The results that followed made that unconventional selection the opening chapter of a long MLB career.

The game was 4-1 in favor of the Brewers, but the Phillies had something <ahem> brewing.
On Wednesday night, needing a victory to help lower their magic number by a game, with one out in the seventh inning, Kyle Schwarber was plunked by pitcher DL Hall, followed by an infield single by Trea Turner. The team had done nothing with runners in scoring position all night long, but any chance that they can get with that happening, they would take it. The lineup card stated that Bryce Harper would stride to the plate as it was his turn in the order. What would he do?
August was Harper's best month of the year. His .333/.496/.573 wasn't his top slugging percentage of this season, but as far as actual production on the field, his 194 wRC+ during the month meant he had few peers during that month in terms of offensive production. While the batting average is nice and the slug is perfectly cromulent, if you're like me, it's the fact that he ended up on base half of the time he came to the plate that astounded. That's treading into Bondsian territory.
It also coincided with a new approach that he and the team took: take pitches. A novel concept, it seemed to have been something that eluded the lineup as an offensive approach for many days. Swinging early and often, attacking pitches if they were in the zone, these were the hallmarks of the Phillies lineup these past few playoff years. In 2026, once August hit, it's as though Harper decided that swinging less, particularly chasing less, was what he wanted to do in order to be more productive at the plate.
And whaddaya know, something crazy happened. Once Harper decided to swing/chase less, he actually started to become more productive at the plate.
Now, I'm not saying that it is a direct corollary that swinging less equals more production at the plate. It clearly has to do with more with the fact that he wasn't chasing pitching out of the zone and getting himself out. But it simply cannot be a coincidence. Harper was good this year for most of the year, the usual cold and hot streaks aside, but during August, he was in a god-like mode when hitting. The team started to win more often too and it seemed like the entire offense was hitting well as a result of Harper swinging a hot bat.
However, it is no coincidence that I left the month of September in those charts.
Look at how the things have flip flopped. He's swinging more and has exited that god mode when at the plate. While he's been fine this month (.278/.346/.375 prior to Wednesday), it's mostly just that – fine. The team has needed him to do more, only for him to not be there. I can't help but believe that his sudden change in approach at the plate – swinging more often – has led to a drop in his production.
Anecdotally, it feels like each time Harper is stepping to the plate, particularly with runners on, he is swinging at the first pitch, no matter where it is. If it also feels to you like he is swinging at missing early in the count more and not just at the first pitch specifically, it could be the fact that pitchers have decided to change their pitch mix to him and he is deciding to jump on the first good fastball he sees.
However, the plan has changed against Harper this year.
There has been a noticeable jump in how pitchers are doing the whole fastball/changeup thing while decreasing the amount of breaking pitches he sees. How has Harper fared against this combination?
You guessed it, by swinging and missing at those offspeed pitches more often.
Granted, it's the natural game of cat and mouse that pitchers and hitters have played since the dawn of the baseball age and Harper is caught in the middle of that. He's still getting hits, but a 300 points loss in OPS is an issue.
The first pitch that Harper saw from Hall in that seventh inning, he drilled straight into the plate back to the pitcher for the second out of the game.
If the Phillies are going to do anything in the playoffs, Bryce Harper needs to be productive at the plate. While he did have good months during the season, August showed that a certain approach at the plate was one that worked for him and led to Phillies wins.
As Jack put it in the season three finale of "Lost", we have to go back.

item.content:encoded:
San Diego Padres third baseman Manny Machado is one of the most accomplished players of this generation, but will he be able to add a World Series title to his star-studded resume?
Bryce Harper. Aaron Judge. Jacob deGrom. Tarik Skubal. Besides being certifiable MLB royalty, what do these players have in common? Despite collectively owning a number of Most Valuable Player and Cy Young Awards, and making a total of 20 playoff appearances over 46 combined seasons, none of them has been able to participate in that final champagne shower of the season, emblematic of the World Series champion.
The list also included third baseman Manny Machado of the San Diego Padres, who, according to the writer, "has been one of the best third basemen in the game for more than a decade," but aside from a 2018 deadline-day trade that sent him from the Baltimore Orioles to the Los Angeles Dodgers, who would lose that year's World Series to the Boston Red Sox, Machado has not otherwise appeared on the game's biggest stage, let alone won the ultimate title.
Still, it's safe to say that Machado has presided over the most successful period in the franchise's history. Since Machado signed with the Padres as a free agent before the 2019 season after 6-1/2 years with the Orioles and two months with the Dodgers, San Diego has made the playoffs four times (2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025).
The Padres also stand on the verge of qualifying again this season, which they can do with a win Wednesday night against the Los Angeles Dodgers and a loss by the Arizona Diamondbacks to the Colorado Rockies. Should they earn an NL wild-card spot, it would be the first time San Diego has made the playoffs three seasons in a row. Not bad for a franchise that made the playoffs a grand total of five times in its 50 years of existence before Machado's arrival.
Machado's contribution to this growing history of success comes in the form of being one of the sport's most reliable players. In his 15th season overall and eighth with the Padres, Machado has been a model of consistency. He's been an All-Star seven times, is a three-time Silver Slugger winner, two-time Gold Glove recipient, has finished in the top 10 in MVP voting five times and compiled a 63.4 career WAR.
Even with all those honors, Machado's most significant "ability" may be his "availability." The only time he's missed any significant time with injury was during his second full season in Baltimore when he appeared in 82 games. Since joining San Diego, Machado has appeared in less than 150 games only once, when he played 138 in 2023, and he even appeared in all 60 games during the COVID-shortened 2020 season.
This year, he's played in 153 of San Diego's 157 games as of Wednesday and, after a stuttering start to the season (.182 average and .616 OPS through May 20), Machado has looked more Manny-like in the ensuing four months. As of Wednesday, he has 28 home runs with 84 RBIs, both of which are within career norms, though his average and OPS (.218 and .710, respectively) are career lows and his 139 strikeouts are a career high.
That being said, with 2,193 hits at the age of 33, Machado is the one active player "with the best chance of reaching 3,000 hits," according to a July 2025 report from The Athletic via The Sporting News. A similar report from MLB.com, also from July 2025, noted that with more than 2,000 hits and 350 home runs at the time, Machado was the 12th player in MLB history to reach those milestones in their age-32 season or earlier. The list includes Hall of Famers Hank Aaron, Lou Gehrig, Mickey Mantle, Willie Mays and Frank Robinson, and contemporaries Miguel Cabrera, Albert Pujols and Alex Rodriguez.
With continued good health and a contract that runs through the 2033 season, Machado will have ample opportunity to join the 3,000-hit/500-HR club, an exclusive group that includes just seven members: Aaron, Mays, Cabrera, Pujols, Rodriguez, Eddie Murray and Rafael Palmeiro.
But that's a discussion for another day. Of more immediate concern, do Machado and the Padres have what it takes to qualify for the playoffs and then make that magical run to a World Series championship? If the playoffs started Wednesday night, they'd travel to meet the Atlanta Braves in the three-game wild-card round. A win there would send them to Los Angeles to take on the Dodgers. Winning that series would match them in the NLCS against one of the Milwaukee Brewers, Chicago Cubs or Philadelphia Phillies. The likeliest World Series opponents would be the Tampa Bay Rays or New York Yankees.
This San Diego squad has definitely been built with a deep playoff run in mind. Michael King, Casey Mize, Robbie Ray and Nick Pivetta headline a solid rotation with the red-hot Fernando Tatis Jr. and Jackson Merrill pacing an offense that has helped the Padres win 13 or their past 15 games going into Wednesday night. The real key to postseason success lies in a shutdown bullpen led by Mason Miller, Adrian Morejon and Bradgley Rodriguez, who has been predicted to be a surprise postseason star.
And don't expect Manny Machado, who has been a foundational piece of this franchise for seven seasons, to be solely along for the ride as the Padres chase World Series glory.

The Philadelphia Phillies have a little bit of work left to do to secure a playoff spot in the National League.
With six games remaining in the regular season, the Phillies hold a four-game lead over the Arizona Diamondbacks. But because they do not possess the tiebreaker, Philadelphia still has a Magic Number of three.
Over the next six games, they need some combination of three victories of their own and losses by the Diamondbacks. They are heavily favored to make the postseason field, but then will be jostling for seeding with the Chicago Cubs, who are currently the No. 1 Wild Card team, and the San Diego Padres, who are currently No. 2.
To catch those teams and make any noise in the playoffs, the Phillies are going to need their stars to play up to their capabilities. Two players they will be counting on to produce are right fielder Bryce Harper and designated hitter Kyle Schwarber.
Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber have been elite against fastballs
In the playoffs, there is a little extra juice when facing opponents. Pitchers are throwing the ball a little harder, and handling velocity becomes a key component for a team to find success. Luckily for Philadelphia, their two star sluggers are among the best in baseball when facing heat.
Some of the nastiest offerings in baseball are off-speed and breaking pitches that can play up a four-seam fastball. So, when a batter gets the opportunity to jump one of those fastballs, they need to make it count.
Harper and Schwarber both accomplish that. As shared by David Adler of MLB.com, thus far in 2026, they are two of the most productive players in the MLB against fastballs. Schwarber is second in the MLB with a batting run value of +30 runs created, which trails only Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros, who has +32.
The Phillies slugger has launched 27 home runs against fastballs this season, which is the most in the MLB. Harper has hit 18 home runs when facing fastballs, and his +28 runs created is the third most in baseball. Willson Contreras of the Boston Red Sox and Ben Rice of the New York Yankees round out the top five with +25 and +23 runs created apiece.
Bryce Harper and Kyle Schwarber produce under brightest lights
While the Philadelphia duo has succeeded against that pitch type, they have also gotten the job done even when the pitcher is throwing with elite velocity. When facing fastballs that are 97 mph or faster this season, Harper has a slugging percentage of .523 with three long balls.
Schwarber has been slightly better, with a .525 slugging percentage and six home runs, which once again leads the MLB.
Even more encouraging for the Phillies is that since the two became teammates, their production against fastballs is even better in the playoffs. Harper has an eye-popping .778 slugging percentage with eight home runs since 2022, making him the best fastball hitter in the MLB postseason during that span.
Schwarber has 10 home runs in the playoffs with a .722 slugging percentage. Hopefully, they keep that production up to help Philadelphia advance in the postseason.

item.content:encoded:
September 22, 2026
The Phillies gave Saturday away, then gave themselves a golden chance to take it back.
But in almost textbook Philadelphia Phillies fashion, they let it go.
Brooks Raley loaded the bases in relief of Andrew Painter one out into the bottom of the sixth, and with a one-run lead, then gave up a Brett Baty liner into center that a diving Justin Crawford could only trap between his glove and the grass for another Mets run scored – and with the bases still full.
Interim manager Don Mattingly yanked Raley as soon as he could for Chase Shugart, and he walked in another to Ronny Mauricio – a .173 hitter at the bottom of the New York order – before a warning-track flyout from Francisco Lindor mercifully ended the frame.
The Phillies set themselves up with a bases-loaded answer of their own in the top of the seventh, after Trea Turner and Alec Bohm drew walks and Luis Arráez singled around a Kyle Schwarber groundout and a Bryce Harper strikeout. But under the pressure situation, Bryson Stott hacked a roller through the grass to second and was left slamming his helmet into the dirt as the Mets jogged back to their dugout without any damage.
The night unraveled from there. The Phillies lost to the Mets, 10-3, up in Queens. Orion Kerkering got tagged for the second straight game, letting up four more runs in the eighth, then was demoted to Triple-A after in a move that essentially exiles the struggling reliever from the roster.
They came back with a 7-2 win the next day, behind a stellar outing from ace Cristopher Sánchez that salvaged a 2-2 split in a four-game series, but with the whole weekend taken into account, it wasn't any kind of silver lining.
The Phillies are supposed to be a playoff team, and still more than likely will be, but they had four games against a Mets club living in the NL East basement right there for the taking. It was the schedule's last gimme. And yet they couldn't help but throw two of those games down the gutter, for little other reason than that they couldn't get out of their own way.
The Phillies were supposed to, or at least wanted fans to think, that they turned over a new leaf at the plate, hitting through August with the kind of small ball approach that their power-heavy lineup went out of its way to avoid for way too long, but they've since reverted back to the old habits and stubborn cold streaks that have long overstayed their welcome.
And the Phillies were supposed to have, or rather praying for, a somewhat stable bullpen after the trade deadline, but now it's so fickle and with so little time left that decisions seem destined to come down to "what starter moves into the bullpen for the postseason?"
It's been this way for five years now, through many big-money contracts that feel like they're never quite living up to the price tag, through many more failed looks at bargain-bin arms, two (and what's looking on track to be three) managerial changes, a dramatic infield shuffle mid-season, and increasingly suspect prospect development that begs an increasingly scarier question of what kind of long-term future does this club really have?
The Phillies aren't a serious baseball team. Not anymore, at least.
They're still good, sure, in the sense that they can – and again, more than likely will – qualify for a spot in October.
But really, they could've locked that spot up a week ago.
Instead, they're 8-10 through September. They punted any possible shot at the NL East title out the window once they let the Braves go 4-3 against them across their final two series, and left a Diamondbacks club that has notoriously broken their hearts before with a faint (and therefore dangerous) glimmer of hope in the final NL Wild Card chase, while leaving a best-of-three road playoff series in Atlanta as the expected prize.
And oh yeah, they do still have to play two good teams that can easily exhaust and bury them before the Phils can even think about any of what might come after.
So where really is the contender in all of this?
Certainly the Phillies are going to lean on their elite starters between Sánchez, Zack Wheeler, a revitalized Aaron Nola, and Jesús Luzardo if they can get him back in time, but at the same time, that wasn't enough against the Mets in the 2024 NLDS or the Dodgers in the 2025 division series a year later. They each countered with shutdown pitching on their side, and hung in there until the Phillies inevitably had to reach into their volatile bullpen to capitalize.
And nothing about the 2026 club suggests that this time would be any different; not when Braves and Dodgers can continue to match them beat for beat talent-wise, while having already proved that they both play much smarter games – in the field, at the plate, and even more so on the base paths – and definitely not after they just showed that they're apparently not that much further above the lowly Mets.
Brandon Marsh, who had an All-Star first half, has one extra-base hit this month.
J.T. Realmuto, once labeled the best catcher in baseball, struck out six times in the Mets series and is a .213 hitter in his mid-30s.
Luis Arráez, who has batted well above .300 for years, suddenly dipped to a .285 average as a Phillie, and while Alec Bohm is impressing with a .328 average through the month, he's never going to hit with the power many hoped for out of a former first-round draft pick at a listed 6'4" and isn't going to suddenly discover it now at age 30 while heading toward free agency.
That leaves Harper and Schwarber as the star sluggers, but at this point, as bats who can be managed around or even directly challenged, while Turner seems to perpetually volley between a $300 million force one minute and a guy who looks like he forgot how to play shortstop the next.
Here's the catch, too: the above names are either in their late 20s at their youngest or pushing well into their 30s on average, after repeated years of trying and failing to out-thump the competition, and with not many more shots expected to be left, especially now that a labor strike puts a serious threat over 2027.
The Phils had a great August, but that was always with a tough September schedule looming, which was always going to tell you what kind of team they really were.
And while there are still six games left, and a probable postseason clinch, there's enough of a picture to tell you this: The Phillies aren't serious.
They haven't been, and really, unless something way more drastic happened at the deadline or Crawford or Painter instantly became the new faces of the franchise, that reality was staring everyone in the face all winter – when the only noticeable difference to the lineup was that Nick Castellanos wasn't in it anymore.
Are they still good enough for October? To get there, sure...probably...hopefully, after this week?
But any further than that? No. They haven't shown anything to say otherwise, or that they're any different from the last two Phillies clubs that hit a hard stop.
